children.text: , this is the landmark of Philippine Art Deco architecture; restored after war damage and long neglect, it reopened on
. You can see the lobby murals and the mango-and-banana ceiling on the free guided tour held every third Sunday of the month or by attending a show.

The Manila Metropolitan Theater is a performance venue that locals simply call the MET. It stands where Padre Burgos Avenue meets Arroceros Street in the Ermita district, beside the Liwasang Bonifacio plaza (formerly Plaza Lawton). Filipino architect Juan M. Arellano, known for the old Legislative Building (now the National Museum of Fine Arts) and the Manila Central Post Office, set aside his usual neoclassicism to design it in the Art Deco style, and it opened on
. Declared a National Historical Landmark in
and a National Cultural Treasure in
, it is the showpiece of Philippine Art Deco architecture.

The theater grew out of a 1920s proposal to build a "people's theater": the City of Manila provided land in Mehan Garden, and a theater company raised the construction money by selling shares to the public. World-famous musicians performed on this stage before the war and shows continued even under the Japanese occupation, but in

the bombing during the Battle of Manila took off the roof and left only the walls. Afterward the building was used as a boxing arena, an ice cream parlor, a bar and a basketball court, and informal settlers moved in. It was repaired in four months and reopened in
on the orders of Imelda Marcos, but after an ownership dispute between the City of Manila and the government insurance agency GSIS it closed in
and lay abandoned for more than 20 years.
The theater came back to life when the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) bought the building in
, paused while the plans were revised because original decorations kept being uncovered, and resumed in
; the aim was to strip away the structures added in 1978 and return the building to Arellano's prewar design. The theater formally reopened on
, its 90th anniversary, and today the NCCA owns and runs it, hosting performances, film screenings and state events. On
the state necrological service for actress and National Artist Nora Aunor was held on this stage.
This is a working theater, not a museum that opens every day. To see the inside you need to join the free guided tour held every third Sunday of the month since

or buy a ticket to a show; on other days you can only view the facade and the night lighting from outside. It suits travelers interested in architecture, modern history and the performing arts. Combine it with the
across the river for a full day in old Manila.

At the center of the facade is a large stained-glass window shaped like a proscenium. Made by the Kraut Art Glass company, it carries the word "metropolitan" among Philippine flowers and leaves and doubles as the theater's sign. On either side, walls of colored tiles resembling Southeast Asian batik curve outward, and bands of zigzag and wavy lines run along the walls.

blocks.title: Spires, iron gates and capiz lamps

children.text: Rows of small finials line the top of the facade, and minaret-like spires rise at both ends of the concave roof. At the entrance, wrought-iron gates worked into leaf patterns alternate with lamps made of capiz shell and pillars shaped like banana leaves. This is where Arellano's approach of blending Western Art Deco with Philippine plants and crafts shows best.

blocks.title: Adam and Eve in the lobby

children.text: The lobby in front of the main theater has a two-story ceiling, with stairways on both sides leading up to the balcony. Beside the stairs stand the bronze sculptures Adam and Eve by Francesco Riccardo Monti, an Italian sculptor who worked in Manila. The drooping floral ironwork of the balustrade was made by the architect's brother, Arcadio Arellano, and the lobby floor is the original from the

High on the walls at either end of the lobby, the murals The Dance and The History of Music by Philippine National Artist Fernando Amorsolo face each other. The ones hanging now are reproductions made during the restoration; the originals have been kept at the GSIS Museum since the theater passed to GSIS in

When you enter the main theater, look up first. Each arched band of the ceiling is lined with painted reliefs of mangoes, banana bunches and tropical leaves, designed by sculptor Isabelo Tampinco. The walls carry lamps modeled on bamboo stalks.
Above the proscenium are eight bas-relief figures by Monti. The restorers had planned to recreate them from old photographs, but in

, when the structures added in the 1978 works were taken down, the original carvings appeared intact. Seating was cut from about 1,600 to 990 when the floor level was adjusted to meet safety standards.

More important than the weather is the theater's calendar. The free tour happens only once a month, on the third Sunday, so it is best to plan your trip around it, and many shows run for only about two days. The theater both first opened and reopened on
, so it is worth checking whether anniversary events are held around that date. In months when the tour falls on Holy Week or a public holiday the date may change, so check the announcements.

Meals before or after a show or tour are eaten in the surrounding area. In the daytime it is good to cross Jones Bridge to Binondo for dumplings, noodles and hopia, or to have Filipino home cooking such as sinigang and adobo at a restaurant in Intramuros. For a quick bite nearby, use the restaurants in the SM City Manila mall beside City Hall or the canteen of the National Museum of Fine Arts. On evening show days it is better to eat before you go in.

To fit the whole facade in one frame, step back across the road toward Liwasang Bonifacio. After dark the stained glass is lit, which makes for good night shots.

Do not miss the back of the building. Two female statues stand on either side of the doorway beneath the tall fly tower. The exotically draped female figures that adorn the theater's exterior are said to be modeled on Siamese (Thai) dancers.
The air conditioning inside is strong, so bring a light jacket, and neat attire is a safe choice on show days.

The Metropolitan Theater is not a tourist site that is open all the time. On days without a tour, show or event you cannot go inside, and the tour schedule and registration method may change, so check the latest notices on the official Facebook page before you go.

Several major roads meet around the theater and traffic is heavy, while the Lawton terminal, the underpass and the train station are always crowded and attract pickpockets. Cross by the underpass and pedestrian crossings and wear your bag in front.
After an evening show the surroundings are dark and nearly deserted. Do not walk; book a Grab in front of the theater.
Photos and video are not allowed during performances. On the tour, follow the guide's instructions on photography and do not use flash.
